bibl.title: In AI We Trust: Ethics, Artificial Intelligence, and Reliability

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: THE WORD `TRUSTWORTHY` IN AI POLICY - whether the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group is entitled to apply it to a machine, tested against the philosophical accounts of what trust is
span.quote: The HLEG state that while trustworthiness is not typically a property ascribed to machines, they want to ascribe it to AI. They propose that there are three main characteristics of trusting AI: The AI technology itself; Designers and organisations behind the development, deployment and use of AI; and The socio-technical systems involved in the AI life cycle

span.label: does AI satisfy the conditions of any account of trust - and if it satisfies only the rational one, is that trust or something else
span.quote: While AI meets all of the requirements of the rational account of trust, it will be shown that this is not actually a type of trust at all, but is instead, a form of reliance.

span.label: a five-part definition of trust, a demonstration that AI fails two of the three accounts, and a PROPOSED RENAMING of a live policy term: `trustworthy AI` should become `reliable AI` or go
span.quote: Therefore, one needs to either change ‘trustworthy AI’ to ‘reliable AI’ or remove it altogether.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Overall, proponents of AI ethics should abandon the ‘trustworthy AI’ paradigm as it is too fraught with problems, replacing it with the reliable AI approach, instead. The field should instead place a greater emphasis on ensuring that organisations using AI, and individuals within those organisations, are trustworthy.

span.label: the anthropomorphisation of machines, and the specific harm of doing it with a MORAL activity rather than a cognitive one
span.quote: One of the main difficulties with analysing the ethical impact of artificial intelligence (AI) is overcoming the tendency to anthropomorphise it. The media is enthralled by images of machines that can do what we can, and often, far better. We are bombarded with novels, movies and television shows depicting sentient robots, so it is not surprising that we associate, categorise, and define these machines in human terms. While people associate human activities and abilities to machines, it becomes problematic when this anthropomorphisation is attached to human moral activities, such as trust.

span.label: conceptual analysis: assemble the rational, affective and normative accounts of trust, reduce them to five characteristics, and check AI against each
span.term: conceptual analysis: assemble the rational, affective and normative accounts of trust, reduce them to five characteristics, and check AI against each
span.quote: Section Three establishes a definition of trust based on five characteristics: A has confidence in B to do X; A believes in the competence of B to do X; A is vulnerable to the actions of B; there is a possibility that B will betray A’s trust; and A believes that B is motivated to do X for affective or normative reasons.

span.label: THE ARGUMENT TURNS ENTIRELY ON TWO OF THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS. AI can satisfy confidence, competence and vulnerability; it cannot satisfy `there is a possibility that B will BETRAY A's trust` nor `B is MOTIVATED to do X for affective or normative reasons`, because it has no emotive states and cannot be held responsible
span.quote: Section Three establishes a definition of trust based on five characteristics: A has confidence in B to do X; A believes in the competence of B to do X; A is vulnerable to the actions of B; there is a possibility that B will betray A’s trust; and A believes that B is motivated to do X for affective or normative reasons.

span.label: and the consequence is a transfer of responsibility, which is the practical stake: `in the normative account, the trustee MUST BE HELD RESPONSIBLE for its actions, WHICH AI CANNOT. Whereas, RELIABLE AI PLACES THE BURDEN OF RESPONSIBILITY ON THOSE DEVELOPING, DEPLOYING, AND USING these technologies`
span.quote: In the normative account, the trustee must be held responsible for its actions, which AI cannot. Whereas, reliable AI places the burden of responsibility on those developing, deploying, and using these technologies.

span.label: the three accounts share confidence, competence and vulnerability and diverge only on betrayal and motive - so the disagreement is located in two components, not in the whole concept
span.quote: The definitions include three characteristics: A has confidence in B to do X; A believes B is competent to do X; A is vulnerable to the actions of B.

span.label: each component is a sliding scale rather than a threshold, so trust can be high on vulnerability and low on confidence at the same time
span.quote: Each of these distinctions is based on a sliding-scale, where there are varying degrees and contexts of trust.

span.label: AI satisfies the first three components and fails the last two, which is why what looks like trust in AI is reliance
span.quote: The following sections will outline the different components within trust definitions and will propose that AI can meet the first three requirements, but fails to meet the last two.

span.label: there can be no breach of trust where there was no confidence to begin with - pessimism about B makes trust impossible rather than merely weak
span.quote: One must have a sense of confidence in the person doing X, because there can be no breach of trust if I am pessimistic that B will do X.

span.label: the paper argues against a live policy document and its own subject term is CONTESTED AT BOTH ENDS: `THE DEFINITION OF AI IS A HIGHLY CONTESTED CONCEPT`, and the account of trust is chosen from three competing ones. The argument is that AI fails `THE MOST PREVALENT DEFINITIONS` - a claim about which definitions are prevalent
span.quote: The definition of AI is a highly contested concept. It often refers to technologies that demonstrate levels of independent intelligence from humans. By its very definition, it is an intelligence that is differentiated from natural intelligence; it is a constructed, artificial, or machine intelligence.

span.label: it is a conceptual argument and offers no empirical claim of its own; the evidence about the HLEG is A WORD COUNT IN A FOOTNOTE - `they use the terms trust, trustworthy, trustworthiness, trusting, and trusted, A TOTAL OF 161 TIMES` in a 39-page document. That is the paper's only measurement and it is not in the body
span.quote: The HLEG consists of 52 industry, civil society and academic experts and was set up by the European Commission to establish ethics guidelines for the development, deployment and use of AI within the European Union. In their 39-page “Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI” document, they use the terms “trust”, “trustworthy”, “trustworthiness”, “trusting”, and “trusted”, a total of 161 times.

span.label: and the remedy is a rename, which the paper does not test: `one needs to EITHER CHANGE trustworthy AI TO reliable AI OR REMOVE IT ALTOGETHER`. Whether substituting the word would change any practice is not addressed
span.quote: Therefore, one needs to either change ‘trustworthy AI’ to ‘reliable AI’ or remove it altogether.

span.label: the paper restricts itself to narrow AI, on the stated grounds that general AI is still speculative
span.quote: The focus of this paper is narrow AI because it is the focus of the HLEG and also because general AI is still speculative.

span.label: the three accounts are not mutually exclusive and may be combined in practice, which the argument acknowledges before separating them
span.quote: The three accounts of trust are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

span.label: AI is checked against ALL THREE accounts of trust rather than the one that suits the conclusion - rational, affective and normative
span.note: eliminates: the objection that the argument depends on picking a demanding definition; AI passes the rational account and the paper says so before disqualifying it on other grounds · outcome: held
span.quote: While AI meets all of the requirements of the rational account of trust, it will be shown that this is not actually a type of trust at all, but is instead, a form of reliance.

span.label: whether `AI` is stable enough to argue about - narrow against general, embodied against not, and robots that have no AI at all
span.note: eliminates: the equivocation between a chatbot and a bomb-disposal robot: `NOT ALL ROBOTS AND DRONES HAVE AI ... only a small percentage of robots have AI` · outcome: held
span.quote: Another important issue is the differentiation between narrow AI and general AI. Narrow AI is a system that is designed and used for specific or limited tasks

span.label: whether the HLEG really means to ascribe trustworthiness to the technology itself, rather than to the people around it
span.note: eliminates: the charitable reading - the paper quotes the HLEG requiring that `ALL ACTORS AND PROCESSES [INCLUDING THE AI TECHNOLOGY ITSELF]` be trustworthy, and notes they acknowledge the property is not typically ascribed to machines · outcome: held

They propose that there are three main characteristics of trusting AI: The AI technology itself; Designers and organisations behind the development, deployment and use of AI; and The socio-technical systems involved in the AI life cycle

span.label: reliance
span.quote: While AI meets all of the requirements of the rational account of trust, it will be shown that this is not actually a type of trust at all, but is instead, a form of reliance.

They propose that there are three main characteristics of trusting AI: The AI technology itself; Designers and organisations behind the development, deployment and use of AI; and The socio-technical systems involved in the AI life cycle

span.label: reliable
span.quote: One can rely on another based on dependable habits, but placing a trust in someone requires they act out of goodwill towards the trustor. This is the main reason why human-made objects, such as AI, can be reliable, but not trustworthy, according to the affective account.

span.label: narrow AI
span.quote: Another important issue is the differentiation between narrow AI and general AI. Narrow AI is a system that is designed and used for specific or limited tasks

span.label: general AI
span.quote: Another important issue is the differentiation between narrow AI and general AI. Narrow AI is a system that is designed and used for specific or limited tasks

span.label: betrayal
span.quote: The affective and normative accounts state that if B does not do X then A may feel betrayed, whereas, this is not included in the rational account.

span.label: vulnerability
span.quote: The definitions include three characteristics: A has confidence in B to do X; A believes B is competent to do X; A is vulnerable to the actions of B.

span.label: goodwill
span.quote: Ultimately, the defining feature of the affective account of trust is that the motivation of B to do X is based on a goodwill towards A.

span.label: misplaced trust
span.quote: Being trustworthy helps in gaining trust, but is neither necessary nor sufficient.

span.label: interpersonal trust
span.quote: This paper proposes a definition of interpersonal trust (A trusts B) found within all three accounts of trust.

span.label: trust, IN FIVE CHARACTERISTICS: A has CONFIDENCE in B to do X; A believes in B's COMPETENCE; A is VULNERABLE to B's actions; there is a possibility B will BETRAY A's trust; and A believes B is MOTIVATED to do X for affective or normative reasons. THE LAST TWO ARE THE ONES AI FAILS
span.quote: Section Three establishes a definition of trust based on five characteristics: A has confidence in B to do X; A believes in the competence of B to do X; A is vulnerable to the actions of B; there is a possibility that B will betray A’s trust; and A believes that B is motivated to do X for affective or normative reasons.

span.label: reliance - WHAT THE RATIONAL ACCOUNT ACTUALLY DESCRIBES. `AI meets all of the requirements of the rational account of trust ... THIS IS NOT ACTUALLY A TYPE OF TRUST AT ALL, BUT IS INSTEAD, A FORM OF RELIANCE`. One can rely on dependable habits; trust requires goodwill
span.quote: While AI meets all of the requirements of the rational account of trust, it will be shown that this is not actually a type of trust at all, but is instead, a form of reliance.

span.label: `trustworthy AI` - A TERM OF ART IN A POLICY DOCUMENT, and the paper's whole target. The HLEG `state that WHILE TRUSTWORTHINESS IS NOT TYPICALLY A PROPERTY ASCRIBED TO MACHINES, THEY WANT TO ASCRIBE IT TO AI` - the term is adopted knowingly, against ordinary usage, exactly as macdonald2015's committee adopted `vaccine hesitancy`
span.quote: The HLEG state that while trustworthiness is not typically a property ascribed to machines, they want to ascribe it to AI. They propose that there are three main characteristics of trusting AI: The AI technology itself; Designers and organisations behind the development, deployment and use of AI; and The socio-technical systems involved in the AI life cycle

span.label: AI - `A HIGHLY CONTESTED CONCEPT`, defined here by contrast (not natural intelligence) and by function (mimicry of tasks that would otherwise need human intelligence), and split into NARROW and GENERAL
span.quote: The definition of AI is a highly contested concept. It often refers to technologies that demonstrate levels of independent intelligence from humans. By its very definition, it is an intelligence that is differentiated from natural intelligence; it is a constructed, artificial, or machine intelligence.

span.label: trust - THE RATIONAL ACCOUNT: a prediction reached by weighing pros and cons, EXPLICITLY UNCONCERNED with why the trustee would act
span.quote: The rational account of trust states that the trustor is making a logical choice, weighing up the pros and cons, when determining whether to place their trust in the trustee.

span.label: trust - THE AFFECTIVE ACCOUNT: the trustee is moved by GOODWILL toward the trustor, and by the very fact of being counted on
span.quote: The affective account of trust states that the trustor places a confidence in, and belief in, the goodwill of the trustee.

span.label: trust - THE NORMATIVE ACCOUNT: the expectation is not what the trustee WILL do but what they OUGHT to do, so failure is betrayal
span.quote: Trust based on the normative account implies that the trustee’s actions will be grounded on what they ought to do .

span.label: quasi trust - Coeckelbergh's sense, where an artefact counts as trusted if it APPEARS as a quasi-other; the paper accepts the description and calls it misplaced trust
span.quote: For example, Mark Coeckelbergh claims that while artefacts, such as AI, do not meet the specific criteria for trust, we may still trust them because ‘they may nevertheless contribute to the establishment of ‘virtual trust’ or ‘quasi trust’ in so far that they appear as quasi-others or social others’ (Coeckelbergh 2012 , p. 57).

span.label: contradicts → the European Commission High-Level Expert Group's `Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI` - the same body floridi2019 counts as evidence of ITS framework's adoption, and of which floridi2019's disclosure says its author is a member
span.quote: The HLEG state that while trustworthiness is not typically a property ascribed to machines, they want to ascribe it to AI. They propose that there are three main characteristics of trusting AI: The AI technology itself; Designers and organisations behind the development, deployment and use of AI; and The socio-technical systems involved in the AI life cycle

span.label: supports → Bryson's position that `AI is not a thing to be trusted. It is a set of software development techniques by which we should be increasing the trustworthiness of our institutions and ourselves`
span.quote: Trusting relationships are those between trusted parties, whereas AI is a systematic group of techniques that enable machines to fulfil particular computing tasks: ‘AI is not a thing to be trusted. It is a set of software development techniques by which we should be increasing the trustworthiness of our institutions and ourselves’

span.label: critiques → Coeckelbergh, that artefacts can bear a `virtual` or `quasi` trust because they appear as quasi-others
span.quote: Certainly, one can say that they trust artefacts, such as AI, but this type of ‘quasi trust’ is actually misplaced trust .

span.label: builds-on → Hall et al. and O'Neill on the separation of trust from trustworthiness
span.quote: The placement of trust in someone often requires a belief about their trustworthiness, but the two are not synonymous: ‘Patients can misplace trust in physicians or institutions that are not deserving, or they can fail to trust those that are’ (Hall et al. 2001 , p. 616).

span.label: and the equivocation is closed before the argument starts: `NOT ALL ROBOTS AND DRONES HAVE AI ... only a small percentage of robots have AI`
span.term: and the equivocation is closed before the argument starts: `NOT ALL ROBOTS AND DRONES HAVE AI ... only a small percentage of robots have AI`
span.quote: However, not all robots and drones have AI. We can also have ‘dumb’ robots, such as those used for bomb disposals, factories, and manufacturing plants. In fact, only a small percentage of robots have AI.

span.label: trust and trustworthiness come apart in both directions - the undeserving are trusted and the deserving are not

span.quote: However, this does not mean that we should distrust AI: ‘In between trust and distrust are found various forms of relying on and taking for granted’ (Jones 1996 , p. 16).
